"'''Call Me'''" is a song by the American [[new wave music|new wave]] band [[Blondie (band)|Blondie]] and the theme to the 1980 film ''[[American Gigolo]]''. Produced and composed by Italian musician [[Giorgio Moroder]], with lyrics by Blondie singer [[Debbie Harry]], the song appeared in the film and its accompanying [[American Gigolo (soundtrack)|soundtrack album]] and was released in the United States in early 1980 as a [[single (music)|single]]. 

"Call Me" was number 1 for six consecutive weeks on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], where it became the band's biggest single and second number 1.<ref name="AG65" /> It also hit number 1 in the UK and Canada, where it became their fourth and second chart-topper, respectively. In the year-end chart of 1980, it was ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]''{{'}}s number 1 single and ''[[RPM (magazine)|RPM]]'' magazine's number 3 in Canada.<ref name="N1" /><ref name="RPM">{{cite web |url= http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/rpm/028020-119.01-e.php?&file_num=nlc008388.0153a&type=1&interval=20&PHPSESSID=u9874ano8k0c5b6bkp4r8qrbp3 |title= Top Singles - Volume 33, No. 6, May 03 1980 |publisher= [[Library and Archives Canada]] |access-date= June 1, 2013 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171025022022/http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/rpm/028020-119.01-e.php?&file_num=nlc008388.0153a&type=1&interval=20&PHPSESSID=u9874ano8k0c5b6bkp4r8qrbp3 |archive-date= October 25, 2017 |url-status= dead |df= mdy-all }}</ref>

"Call Me" is a song by the American new wave band Blondie and the theme to the 1980 film American Gigolo. Produced and composed by Italian musician Giorgio Moroder, with lyrics by Blondie singer Debbie Harry, the song appeared in the film and its accompanying soundtrack album and was released in the United States in early 1980 as a single. 

"Call Me" was number 1 for six consecutive weeks on the Billboard Hot 100, where it became the band's biggest single and second number 1. It also hit number 1 in the UK and Canada, where it became their fourth and second chart-topper, respectively. In the year-end chart of 1980, it was Billboard{{'}}s number 1 single and RPM magazine's number 3 in Canada.

sections.heading: Background and recording
sections.wikitext:
In 2014, keyboardist-composer [[Harold Faltermeyer]] remembered the recording process as having three main sections: first [[Giorgio Moroder]] and his music crew recorded an instrumental version of the song at [[Westlake Recording Studios]] in [[Los Angeles]], with the tape locked to [[SMPTE timecode]] so that it would synchronize with the film. Then the project moved to [[New York City|New York]] for the Blondie recording session, at which the band surprised Moroder by insisting they would play their own parts. Faltermeyer was engineering when [[Debbie Harry]] sang and [[Chris Stein]] played electric guitar. Stein's guitar and amplifier were buzzing and noisy, so his setup was repaired to get a clean recording. The band had difficulty locking to sync, so Moroder stopped the unfinished sessions to save time and took the project back to Los Angeles to more quickly add the final parts with his own picked musicians, including a keyboard solo by Faltermeyer.<ref name="Faltermeyer2014">{{cite web |url=https://www.redbullmusicacademy.com/lectures/harold-faltermeyer-tokyo-2014 |date=2014 |title=Harold Faltermeyer: Red Bull Music Academy lecture |last=Schmidt |first=Torsten |website=Red Bull Music |access-date=May 23, 2021}}</ref>

On the [[American Gigolo (soundtrack)|''American Gigolo'' soundtrack]] album, Blondie the band is credited only for vocals, with other credits naming Moroder's crew of [[Keith Forsey]] on drums/percussion and Faltermeyer on keyboards and arrangements.<ref>{{cite AV media |title=[[American Gigolo (soundtrack)|American Gigolo]] |type=credits |date=1980 |publisher=[[Polydor Records]] |id=PD-1-6259}}</ref> Faltermeyer said the band was angry about being replaced by session players but the song turned out to be very successful, so they took it in stride. Blondie keyboard player [[Jimmy Destri]] did not like Faltermeyer's solo and would have preferred his own version.<ref name="Faltermeyer2014" />
sections.text:
In 2014, keyboardist-composer Harold Faltermeyer remembered the recording process as having three main sections: first Giorgio Moroder and his music crew recorded an instrumental version of the song at Westlake Recording Studios in Los Angeles, with the tape locked to SMPTE timecode so that it would synchronize with the film. Then the project moved to New York for the Blondie recording session, at which the band surprised Moroder by insisting they would play their own parts. Faltermeyer was engineering when Debbie Harry sang and Chris Stein played electric guitar. Stein's guitar and amplifier were buzzing and noisy, so his setup was repaired to get a clean recording. The band had difficulty locking to sync, so Moroder stopped the unfinished sessions to save time and took the project back to Los Angeles to more quickly add the final parts with his own picked musicians, including a keyboard solo by Faltermeyer.

On the American Gigolo soundtrack album, Blondie the band is credited only for vocals, with other credits naming Moroder's crew of Keith Forsey on drums/percussion and Faltermeyer on keyboards and arrangements. Faltermeyer said the band was angry about being replaced by session players but the song turned out to be very successful, so they took it in stride. Blondie keyboard player Jimmy Destri did not like Faltermeyer's solo and would have preferred his own version.

sections.heading: Composition and lyrics
sections.wikitext:
"Call Me" was composed by Italian disco producer Giorgio Moroder as the main theme song of the 1980 film ''[[American Gigolo]]''. It is played in the key of [[D minor]] with a [[tempo]] of 143 beats per minute,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Key & BPM for Call Me by Blondie |url=https://tunebat.com/Info/Call-Me-Blondie/7HKxTNVlkHsfMLhigmhC0I |access-date=11 June 2023 |website=Tunebat}}</ref> with Debbie Harry's vocals ranging from [[C (musical note)|C<sub>4</sub>]] to [[E (musical note)|E<sub>5</sub>]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Giorgio |first1=Moroder |last2=Blondie |date=2002-03-05 |title=Call Me |url=https://www.musicnotes.com/sheetmusic/mtd.asp?ppn=MN0040070 |access-date=2023-06-11 |website=Musicnotes.com |language=en}}</ref> Moroder originally asked [[Stevie Nicks]] from [[Fleetwood Mac]] to perform a song for the soundtrack but she was prevented because of a recently signed contract with [[Modern Records (1980)|Modern Records]]. Moroder turned to Debbie Harry of Blondie, presenting Harry with an instrumental track called "Man Machine". Harry was asked to write the lyrics, a process that Harry states took a mere few hours.<ref>100 Greatest Songs of the 80s, Episode 2, VH1</ref> The lyrics were written from the perspective of the main character in the film, male [[Prostitution|prostitute]] Julian Kay ([[Richard Gere]]).<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Bockris |first=Victor |date=May 24, 1980 |title=Dinner with Blondie... and William Burroughs |url=https://www.rocksbackpages.com/Library/Article/dinner-with-blondie-and-william-burroughs |magazine=New Music News |location=New York |access-date=May 30, 2017 |quote=Harry: Giorgio's original idea was to call it "man machine" because the man was just like the sex machine. Stein: Debbie's lyrics are much more subtle than the ones he wrote. His thing was very direct like saying I am a man and I go out and I fuck all the girls. Debbie's lyrics are a lot more subtle and the movie in a way is not that blatant, it is sort of subtle. Harry: It was like teasing too because the thing about the movie was that he was always—'Call me! Call me if you want me to come to you.' And it was like these little commands had this macho quality through his being a male hooker, you know that kind of demanding business.}}</ref> 
{{Listen
 | title = "Call Me"
 | filename = BlondieCallMe.ogg
 | pos = left
 | description = [[Debbie Harry]] wrote the song's lyrics; she was coached by composer [[Giorgio Moroder]] to add some Italian- and French-language phrases including "Amore, chiamami" and "Appelle-moi, mon chéri".<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/blondie-debbie-harry-isolated-vocals-call-me-1980/ |title=Listen to Debbie Harry's incredible isolated vocal track on Blondie's hit 'Call Me' |author=Staff |date=2020 |magazine=Far Out |access-date=May 23, 2021}}</ref>
}}
Harry said the lyrics were inspired by her visual impressions from watching the film and that "When I was writing it, I pictured the opening scene, driving on the coast of California."<ref>{{cite journal|author= Tamara Warren |title= Mustang Debbie: Blondie's Legendary Lead Singer Confesses a Love of Cars |journal=[[Autoweek]] |date= July 9, 2012 |volume= 62 |issue= 14 |pages= 42–44 |issn= 0192-9674}}</ref> The completed song was then recorded by the band, with Moroder producing. The bridge of the original English-language version also includes Harry saying "call me" in two European languages: {{Langx|it|text=Amore, chiamami|translation=Love, call me}} and {{Langx|fr|text=Appelle-moi, mon chéri|translation=Call me, my darling}}.
sections.text:
"Call Me" was composed by Italian disco producer Giorgio Moroder as the main theme song of the 1980 film American Gigolo. It is played in the key of D minor with a tempo of 143 beats per minute, with Debbie Harry's vocals ranging from C<sub>4</sub> to E<sub>5</sub>. Moroder originally asked Stevie Nicks from Fleetwood Mac to perform a song for the soundtrack but she was prevented because of a recently signed contract with Modern Records. Moroder turned to Debbie Harry of Blondie, presenting Harry with an instrumental track called "Man Machine". Harry was asked to write the lyrics, a process that Harry states took a mere few hours. The lyrics were written from the perspective of the main character in the film, male prostitute Julian Kay (Richard Gere). 
{{Listen
 | title = "Call Me"
 | filename = BlondieCallMe.ogg
 | pos = left
 | description = Debbie Harry wrote the song's lyrics; she was coached by composer Giorgio Moroder to add some Italian- and French-language phrases including "Amore, chiamami" and "Appelle-moi, mon chéri".
}}
Harry said the lyrics were inspired by her visual impressions from watching the film and that "When I was writing it, I pictured the opening scene, driving on the coast of California." The completed song was then recorded by the band, with Moroder producing. The bridge of the original English-language version also includes Harry saying "call me" in two European languages: {{Langx|it|text=Amore, chiamami|translation=Love, call me}} and {{Langx|fr|text=Appelle-moi, mon chéri|translation=Call me, my darling}}.

sections.heading: Release
sections.wikitext:
In the US, the song was released by three record companies: the longest version (at 8:06) on the [[American Gigolo (soundtrack)|soundtrack album]] by [[Polydor Records|Polydor]], the 7" and 12" on Blondie's label [[Chrysalis Records|Chrysalis]] and a Spanish-language 12" version, with lyrics by Buddy and Mary McCluskey, on the disco label [[Salsoul Records]]. A Spanish-language version, titled "Llámame", was meant for release in Mexico and some South American countries. This version was also released in the US and the UK and had its CD debut on Chrysalis/[[EMI]]'s rarities compilation ''[[Blonde and Beyond]]'' (1993). In 1988, a remixed version by [[Ben Liebrand]] taken from the Blondie remix album ''[[Once More into the Bleach]]'' was issued as a single in the UK. In 2001, the "original long version" appeared as a bonus track on the ''[[Autoamerican]]'' album re-issue.

In 2014, Blondie re-recorded the song for their compilation album ''Greatest Hits Deluxe Redux''. The compilation was part of a 2-disc set called ''[[Blondie 4(0) Ever]]'' which included their tenth studio album ''Ghosts of Download'' and marked the 40th anniversary of the forming of the band.

Harry recorded an abbreviated version of the song that was backed by the Muppet Band for her guest appearance on ''[[The Muppet Show]]'' in August 1980. It was first broadcast in January 1981.<ref>{{cite web |title=Debbie Harry - Call Me [HD] |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dfBx2ggAHbs |website=Youtube.com | date=April 13, 2022 |publisher=Muppet Songs |access-date=September 21, 2023}}</ref>

In the US, the song was released by three record companies: the longest version (at 8:06) on the soundtrack album by Polydor, the 7" and 12" on Blondie's label Chrysalis and a Spanish-language 12" version, with lyrics by Buddy and Mary McCluskey, on the disco label Salsoul Records. A Spanish-language version, titled "Llámame", was meant for release in Mexico and some South American countries. This version was also released in the US and the UK and had its CD debut on Chrysalis/EMI's rarities compilation Blonde and Beyond (1993). In 1988, a remixed version by Ben Liebrand taken from the Blondie remix album Once More into the Bleach was issued as a single in the UK. In 2001, the "original long version" appeared as a bonus track on the Autoamerican album re-issue.

In 2014, Blondie re-recorded the song for their compilation album Greatest Hits Deluxe Redux. The compilation was part of a 2-disc set called Blondie 4(0) Ever which included their tenth studio album Ghosts of Download and marked the 40th anniversary of the forming of the band.

Harry recorded an abbreviated version of the song that was backed by the Muppet Band for her guest appearance on The Muppet Show in August 1980. It was first broadcast in January 1981.

sections.heading: Reception
Music video
sections.wikitext:
There were two videos made:
* One was clips and video footage of Debbie Harry in New York City. The video can be found on the 1991 UK video compilation ''[[The Complete Picture: The Very Best of Deborah Harry and Blondie]]''.
* The other, which came out in 1981, did not feature any of the band. It depicted a New York City taxi driver (who had appeared in several other Blondie music videos) driving his [[Checker Taxi]] through [[Manhattan]] traffic. This version was part of ''[[The Best of Blondie]]'' compilation video in 1981.

sections.heading: Notable samples & covers
sections.wikitext:
* A version of this song appeared on the 1980 album ''[[Chipmunk Punk]]'' by [[the Chipmunks]].<ref name=allmusic>{{AllMusic | class= album | id= mw0000874302 | title= ''Chipmunk Punk'' | first= Doug | last= Stone | accessdate= 5 June 2020}}</ref>
* In 1996, Australian heavy metal band [[Dungeon (band)|Dungeon]] released a cover of the song on their first album ''Demolition''. The song was re-recorded for the band's Japan tour CD ''Rising Power'' in 2003.
* In 2022, [[electronic dance music]] producers [[Gabry Ponte]], [[R3hab]] and [[Timmy Trumpet]] released a cover of the song.<ref>{{cite news |title=Gabry Ponte, R3HAB And Timmy Trumpet Team Up For 'Call Me' {{!}} UFO Network |url=https://ufo-network.com/2022/01/17/gabry-ponte-r3hab-and-timmy-trumpet-call-me/ |access-date=January 26, 2023 |work=[[UFO Network]] |date=January 17, 2022}}</ref> It peaked at No. 80 on the [[Dutch Single Top 100]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hung |first1=Steffen |title=Gabry Ponte x R3Hab x Timmy Trumpet - Call Me |url=https://dutchcharts.nl/showitem.asp?interpret=Gabry+Ponte+x+R3Hab+x+Timmy+Trumpet&titel=Call+Me&cat=s |website=hitparade.ch |access-date=January 26, 2023}}</ref>
*In September 2023, U2's single Atomic City credited Harry/Moroder as co writers on the track given the clear inspiration of Call Me.
*In June 2024, German [[europop]] group ''[[Cascada]]'' released a cover of the song as the second single from their 5th studio album Studio 24.
*The song was heard in the first trailer for the 2026 superhero film ''[[Supergirl (2026 film)|Supergirl]]''.
sections.text:
* A version of this song appeared on the 1980 album Chipmunk Punk by the Chipmunks.
* In 1996, Australian heavy metal band Dungeon released a cover of the song on their first album Demolition. The song was re-recorded for the band's Japan tour CD Rising Power in 2003.
* In 2022, electronic dance music producers Gabry Ponte, R3hab and Timmy Trumpet released a cover of the song. It peaked at No. 80 on the Dutch Single Top 100.
*In September 2023, U2's single Atomic City credited Harry/Moroder as co writers on the track given the clear inspiration of Call Me.
*In June 2024, German europop group Cascada released a cover of the song as the second single from their 5th studio album Studio 24.
*The song was heard in the first trailer for the 2026 superhero film Supergirl.
